Image via Paramount Pictures By Hannah Hunt Published Oct 30, 2025 Back in 2021, Hannah’s love of all things nerdy collided with her passion for writing — and she hasn’t stopped since. She covers pop culture news, writes reviews, and conducts interviews on just about every kind of media imaginable. If she’s not talking about something spooky, she’s talking about gaming, and her favorite moments in anything she’s read, watched, or played are always the scariest ones. For Hannah, nothing beats the thrill of discovering what’s lurking in the shadows or waiting around the corner for its chance to go bump in the night. Once described as “strictly for the sickos,” she considers it the highest of compliments. Sign in to your Collider account Summary Generate a summary of this story follow Follow followed Followed Like Like Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap When Alien premiered in 1979, it didn’t just redefine science fiction — it detonated a fusion of horror and sci-fi that filmmakers have been chasing ever since. Ridley Scott ’s masterpiece combined blue-collar space realism with primal terror, setting the standard for how to make the unknown feel close enough to touch. The xenomorph wasn’t just a monster, it was a reflection of human fragility in the face of something vast, cold, and indifferent. The result was a film that terrified audiences not only because of what they could see, but because of what they couldn’t . Since then, the sci-fi horror genre has evolved into a thriving playground for existential dread. Some of these films lean into cosmic horror, some into body horror, and others into the slow rot of human sanity in isolation. What they all share is an understanding that the most frightening thing about space, or science itself, isn\'t technology. It’s the scale of what we don’t understand. These ten films don’t just stand on the shoulders of Alien — they carve out their own nightmares in the dark . They prove that sci-fi horror remains one of the most enduring, imaginative, and terrifying corners of cinema. 10 ‘Annihilation’ (2018) Alex Garland ’s Annihilation is a sci-fi horror odyssey that fuses cosmic terror with intimate, psychological unraveling. When a mysterious phenomenon known as “The Shimmer” begins warping everything it touches, a team of scientists ventures inside — and encounters a world that defies logic. It’s a film about mutation, impermanence, and what happens when human identity is swallowed by something larger. The creature design is mesmerizing and horrific, from the eerie mutated bear to the film’s final, wordless confrontation with a doppelgänger. Garland’s direction leans into disorientation, making time, space, and identity feel fluid. It’s as much about confronting oneself as it is about facing the unknown. The film’s horror isn’t loud; it’s creeping and inescapable. Natalie Portman anchors it with a performance full of quiet, haunted resolve. Annihilation doesn\'t end with neat answers, but with a sense of inevitability — that the alien isn’t just “out there,” but already reshaping us. It’s as terrifying as it is beautiful. 9 ‘Life’ (2017) A broken space helmet spattered with blood, and a hand pressing up against the visor from the inside in Life. Image via Columbia Pictures Daniel Espinosa ’s Life wears its influences proudly — it’s a lean, mean creature feature in the vein of Alien , but with its own cruel streak. When an international crew aboard the ISS discovers a rapidly evolving organism, scientific wonder quickly turns to horror. The creature, nicknamed Calvin, is both terrifyingly simple and devastatingly efficient, forcing the crew into a brutal fight for survival. What sets Life apart is its relentless pace. It wastes no time plunging into chaos, and once it starts, it doesn’t let up. The film uses the cramped, zero-gravity environment to build tension, turning even routine maneuvers into life-or-death struggles. Its kills are shocking in their precision, and the film isn’t afraid to punish its characters or the audience with a gut-punch of an ending. It may not have rewritten the genre, but Life excels at what it sets out to do: trap viewers in a tight, airless nightmare and let the monster hunt. Sometimes, that’s all you need to be terrifying. 8 ‘Under the Skin’ (2013) Jonathan Glazer ’s Under the Skin is an alien invasion story stripped to its most disturbing essence. Scarlett Johansson plays a creature wearing human skin, prowling the streets of Scotland in search of prey. There are no expository monologues, no world-ending stakes. Instead, Glazer uses minimalism, eerie soundscapes, and dreamlike imagery to make the familiar feel completely alien. The film is as much about perspective as it is about horror. By showing the world through the alien’s cold, observational lens, everything human becomes uncanny. Victims are lured into black, inky voids where their bodies are consumed and hollowed out. Johansson’s performance is chilling in its detachment — and devastating when cracks of something resembling empathy start to show. Under the Skin isn’t traditionally “scary” in the jump-scare sense. Its horror is quieter, stranger, and deeper. It unsettles because it denies us comfort, forcing us to see humanity from the outside. It’s one of the most haunting films of the 21st century, a perfect marriage of science fiction and existential dread. 7 ‘Prometheus’ (2012) With Prometheus , Scott returned to the universe he helped shape — not to give answers, but to raise terrifying new questions. The film follows a team of explorers seeking humanity’s creators on a distant moon, only to uncover something far older and far less merciful. This is cosmic horror in its purest form : elegant, intellectual, and merciless. The film’s design is breathtaking, blending sleek futuristic technology with ancient, alien architecture. But beneath that beauty is rot. Scott weaponizes scale — massive structures dwarf the human explorers, making them feel small and insignificant against forces they can’t comprehend. The infamous “medpod” scene, in which Noomi Rapace ’s character performs emergency surgery on herself to remove an alien organism, remains one of the most harrowing body horror moments of the 2010s. Though divisive, Prometheus thrives on dread rather than cheap shocks. It’s about humanity’s hunger for meaning, and what happens when the answer is something indifferent and cruel . 6 ‘Pandorum’ (2009) Antje Traue as Nadia in Pandorum Image via Constantine Film Christian Alvart ’s Pandorum is a grimy, under-the-radar gem that blends psychological dread with feral, creature-driven terror. Set aboard a massive colonization ship drifting through deep space, the story follows two crew members ( Dennis Quaid and Ben Foster ) who awaken from hypersleep to find the vessel seemingly abandoned — except for the horrors lurking in the dark. The film builds its scares through disorientation. With memory loss, unreliable narrators, and a labyrinthine ship, every hallway feels like a trap. The monsters — once human — are a brutal evolution gone wrong, their presence amplifying the sense of claustrophobia. Meanwhile, the creeping paranoia about what really happened on the ship gives the story its psychological edge. Drawing inspiration from Alien and Event Horizon but carving out its own identity, Pandorum thrives on atmosphere. Its lighting is oppressive, its sound design sharp, and its revelations deeply unsettling. It may not have the fame of its predecessors, but it’s a terrifying, effective reminder that in the void, humanity can become its own worst monster . 5 ‘Cloverfield’ (2008) Matt Reeves ’ Cloverfield brought creature features into the digital age with unflinching immediacy. Shot entirely in found-footage style, the film drops viewers into the middle of a New York City under siege by a colossal, unknown monster. By focusing on a group of ordinary people rather than soldiers or scientists, it transforms an apocalyptic event into something terrifyingly intimate. The lack of exposition is key to its horror. We don’t know where the monster came from or what it wants, we only know what the camera can capture. Reeves turns shaky, handheld footage into a weapon, creating a visceral sense of panic and disorientation. Set pieces like the tunnel attack and the helicopter crash remain standout moments in modern horror. Beyond spectacle, Cloverfield works because it’s grounded in human fear — the desperate need to survive, to find the people you love, even as the world collapses. It’s a landmark in both sci-fi horror and the found-footage subgenre, proving that the scariest monsters are often the ones you can’t fully see. 4 ‘Sunshine’ (2007) Danny Boyle ’s Sunshine begins as hard sci-fi — a mission to reignite a dying sun — and ends as a psychological descent into cosmic terror. The film follows a crew traveling toward a star, tasked with detonating a massive bomb to save Earth. But the true danger isn’t just the mission itself; it’s the isolation, pressure, and the inhuman scale of their surroundings slowly eroding their sanity. Boyle builds the tension with meticulous pacing, immersing us in the sterile, claustrophobic corridors of the Icarus II. As the mission falters and a mysterious presence begins to manifest, the film transforms. Its shift from scientific precision to near-mythic horror is intentional — confronting viewers with the overwhelming insignificance of humanity against a star’s fury. Cillian Murphy , Rose Byrne , and Chris Evans ground the story with raw, human performances. Sunshine refuses easy answers, instead letting its terror seep through silence, awe, and the sheer brutality of space. It’s a visually stunning, existentially chilling entry in the sci-fi horror canon. 3 ‘Event Horizon’ (1997) In Paul W.S. Anderson ’s Event Horizon , the vastness of space isn’t the real terror — it’s what waits beyond it. A rescue crew boards the Event Horizon, a starship that vanished during a faster-than-light experiment and has now mysteriously returned. What they discover is worse than mechanical failure: the ship has passed through a dimension of pure, incomprehensible chaos, bringing something unspeakable back with it. What begins as a sci-fi mystery quickly warps into a cosmic nightmare. Sam Neill delivers a chilling performance as Dr. Weir, whose unraveling mirrors the ship’s own descent into hell. The production design turns the vessel into a cathedral of madness — all steel, shadows, and hidden horrors. Anderson doesn’t shy away from gore, using shocking bursts of violence to punctuate an oppressive atmosphere. While initially divisive, Event Horizon has become a cult classic for good reason. It blends haunted house horror with deep-space science fiction, tapping into a uniquely unsettling fear: that some doors aren’t meant to be opened. It’s brutal, unrelenting, and unforgettable — the kind of movie that lingers long after the credits roll. 2 ‘The Fly’ (1986) David Cronenberg ’s The Fly transforms scientific ambition into a slow-motion tragedy. Jeff Goldblum stars as Seth Brundle, a brilliant but impulsive scientist who accidentally fuses his DNA with a housefly during a teleportation experiment. What begins as a thrilling scientific breakthrough quickly unravels into body horror of the highest order. Cronenberg doesn’t just show Brundle’s transformation — he makes us feel it, inch by inch, as skin, bone, and identity rot away. Goldblum delivers one of the best performances of his career, bringing both manic energy and devastating vulnerability to Brundle’s descent. Geena Davis grounds the story emotionally, making the horror feel painfully human. The practical effects are unforgettable: teeth fall out, skin sloughs away, and Brundle becomes something unrecognizable. What elevates The Fly beyond its monstrous imagery is its tragic heart. It’s a love story poisoned by science and obsession, a reminder that curiosity can turn cruel when it pushes past nature’s boundaries. It remains one of the most affecting, unforgettable entries in sci-fi horror history. 1 ‘The Thing’ (1982) John Carpenter’s The Thing is a paranoia bomb. Set in the frozen isolation of Antarctica, the film traps a small group of researchers with an alien organism capable of perfectly imitating its victims. As trust erodes and suspicion spreads, the real monster becomes the fear of not knowing who is human. Rob Bottin ’s revolutionary practical effects remain some of the most grotesquely impressive creature work ever put to screen, giving the alien’s transformations a tactile, revolting realism that CGI still struggles to match. Carpenter uses silence and space as weapons, letting long stretches of tension build until they snap with shocking violence. The film’s famously ambiguous ending — with Kurt Russell ’s MacReady and Keith David ’s Childs staring each other down as the camp burns — leaves audiences with a cold, lingering dread. The Thing was underappreciated in its time, but today it’s widely considered a masterclass in both horror and science fiction. It’s not just a creature feature — it’s a study in fear, trust, and what happens when survival demands certainty that doesn’t exist. From sweeping fantasy epics to gritty crime sagas the best movie trilogies represent storytelling at its most ambitious and satisfying. These aren\'t just three films released one after the other – they\'re carefully constructed narrative arcs that build worlds, explore core themes, and deliver emotional payoffs that single films simply can\'t match. The greatest film trilogies work because they understand the classic three-act storytelling structure: the introduction, the escalation, and the resolution. Whether it\'s watching a young farmboy become a Jedi Knight across a galaxy far, far away, following a teenager\'s adventures through time and space, or witnessing the rise and fall of a mafia family across generations, the best trilogy movies give us room to breathe, grow attached, and experience genuine transformation alongside their characters. What makes certain trilogies endure while others fade? Sometimes it\'s the visionary director who maps out all three chapters from the start. Other times, it\'s the unexpected alchemy of a sequel that deepens what came before, transforming a standalone hit into something greater. We started by asking you, Empire \'s passionate readers, to vote for your favourite all-time movie trilogies. Thousands of you responded, championing everything from pure three-film series untouched by prequels or sequels, to specific trios within longer franchises, to triptychs that were intended to be evaluated as a threesome even if they don’t share the same cast or characters. Where a coherent narrative across three films existed, we counted it – which is why you\'ll find certain trilogies here even when fourth or fifth instalments later emerged. Once your votes were in, we turned to Empire \'s experienced team of critics and contributors, asking them to weigh in with their expertise on the artistic merit, cultural impact, and lasting influence of each trilogy. We evaluated how well each trilogy functions as a complete narrative – does the third film stick the landing? Does the middle chapter avoid the sophomore slump? FASCINATING FACT: Mortensen patched up his own costume while filming and, when he lost a tooth in an orc-based squabble, he simply had it glued back in. 014 Captain Jack sparrow APPEARANCES: The Pirates Of The Caribbean series (2003-2011) CREATORS: Ted Elliott, Terry Rossio PERFORMER: Johnny Depp DEFINING MOMENT: His panicked cry of, “But why is the rum gone?” on learning that fellow castaway Elizabeth Swann (Keira Knightley) has created a rum-fuelled beacon to attract rescue. FASCINATING FACT: Elliott and Rossio designed Cap’n Jack in the spirit of characters in classic literature and opera like Figaro; the comic, puckish counterpoint to the film’s heroes. 013 Iron Man APPEARANCES: The Marvel Cinematic Universe (2008-2015) CREATORS: Stan Lee, Don Heck, Jack Kirby, Larry Lieber PERFORMER: Robert Downey Jr. DEFINING MOMENT: At a press conference to deny that he is Iron Man, Tony Stark leans into the mic and announces: “I am Iron Man.” It’s the move of a billionaire genius playboy philanthropist, and narcissist, and dispensed with all that secret identity baloney right off the bat. FASCINATING FACT: Iron Man had been years in development, with Nicolas Cage and Tom Cruise linked to the role. 012 Marty McFly APPEARANCES: Back To The Future trilogy (1985-1990) CREATORS: Robert Zemeckis, Bob Gale PERFORMER: Michael J. Fox DEFINING MOMENT: After belting out Johnny B. Goode: “I guess you guys aren’t ready for that yet, but your kids are gonna love it.” FASCINATING FACT: As Calvin Klein was relatively unknown in Europe at the time, Marty is mistaken for Levi Strauss and Pierre Cardin in some Euro versions. 011 Michael Corleone APPEARANCES: The Godfather trilogy (1972-1990) CREATOR: Mario Puzo PERFORMER: Al Pacino DEFINING MOMENT: Watch him steeling himself to kill Sollozzo and Capt. McCluskey in the restaurant – a journey to the dark side begins. FASCINATING FACT: Michael Corleone is a bit-part player in Puzo’s novel The Sicilian. 010 The Dude APPEARANCE: The Big Lebowski (1998) CREATORS: Joel Coen, Ethan Coen PERFORMER: Jeff Bridges DEFINING MOMENT: Throughout, The Dude is striving to return to his habitual state of rest but fails. Driving his beat-up Torino home in a rare moment of contentment, supping a beer, taking a toke and singing along to Creedence on the eight-track, he spots he’s being trailed. This latest assault on his embattled karma causes him in quick succession to flick his joint into his lap, squeal like a girl, pour beer on his trousers, and slam the Torino into a row of dustbins. Rattled but unhurt, his drugstore Ray-Bans — an excellent bellwether for The Dude’s equilibrium — are left comically askew. FASCINATING FACT: With the exception of his dream, you never actually see The Dude bowl. 009 Darth Vader APPEARANCES: Star Wars: Episodes III-VI (1977-2005) CREATOR: George Lucas PERFORMERS: David Prowse, James Earl Jones (voice), Sebastian Shaw, Hayden Christensen DEFINING MOMENT: In the first two films (i.e. Episodes IV and V), Lord Vader is nothing more — or less — than the ultimate, über-cool villain. Remorseless, fearless, able to force-strangle his underlings via video link... But it’s in Return Of The Jedi that we realise, somehow, that we care about Vader — just as Luke does. In this sense, he’s defined by a small exchange with his offspring. Having been urged to let go of his hate, he says, almost sadly, “It is too late for me, son...” FASCINATING FACT: Vader was also technically played by famed Hollywood sword-master Bob Anderson, who donned the suit for Episode V and VI’s lightsaber duels. 008 Tyler Durden APPEARANCE: Fight Club (1999) CREATOR: Chuck Palahniuk PERFORMER: Brad Pitt DEFINING MOMENT: Tyler delivering the rules is the most quoted moment, but the scene that captures his dark humour is when he invites a beating from bar-owner Lou, spraying blood over him with an evilly gleeful, “You don’t know where I’ve been!” FASCINATING FACT: Pitt originally wanted to play The Narrator, but David Fincher convinced him to be Tyler instead. 007 John McClane APPEARANCES: The Die Hard films (1988-2013), National Lampoon’s Loaded Weapon 1 (1993) CREATORS: Roderick Thorp, Steven E. de Souza, Jeb Stuart PERFORMER: Bruce Willis DEFINING MOMENT: Sending a dead terrorist back to his cohorts with a zinger daubed on him in blood, in what is officially a Christmas movie . Tough, cocky, darkly funny. FASCINATING FACT: Fox had to offer the role to Frank Sinatra first, as technically Die Hard is a sequel to 1968’s The Detective. 006 The Joker APPEARANCES: Batman The Movie (1966), Batman (1989), Batman: Mask Of The Phantasm (1993), The Dark Knight (2008) CREATORS: Jerry Robinson, Bill Finger, Bob Kane PERFORMERS: Cesar Romero, Mark Hamill (voice), Jack Nicholson, Heath Ledger DEFINING MOMENT: Most votes specified Ledger’s Oscar-winning take, so we’ll go with his pencil-disappearing “magic trick”. Nasty and deeply unpredictable. FASCINATING FACT: Ledger’s Joker never looks at his victims while killing them. 005 Ellen Ripley APPEARANCE: The Alien quadrilogy (1979-1997) CREATORS: Walter Hill, David Giler, Ron Cobb, Dan O’Bannon PERFORMER: Sigourney Weaver DEFINING MOMENT: With a survival instinct to match her xenomorphic nemesis, Ripley is one of nature’s rationalists. Indeed, had they followed her hard-nosed attempt to uphold quarantine rules and prevent the stricken Kane being brought back on board — “If we let it in, the ship could be infected” — the Nostromo crew, if not Kane, would remain a whole lot healthier. FASCINATING FACT: In the process of considering Meryl Streep for the role of Ripley, Ridley Scott was stopped in his tracks by the sight of Weaver in thigh-high boots, bursting into his office, half an hour late for her audition. 004 Batman APPEARANCES: Batman (1966), Batman (1989), Batman Returns (1992), Batman Forever (1995), Batman & Robin (1997), Batman Begins (2005), The Dark Knight (2008), The Dark Knight Rises (2012) CREATORS: Bob Kane, Bill Finger PERFORMERS: Adam West, Michael Keaton, Val Kilmer, George Clooney, Christian Bale DEFINING MOMENT: It really should be from Christian Bale’s Dark Knight, when he is going fist to face with the Joker as Gordon (Gary Oldman) looks on fretting, “Who’s in control?” Good question. FASCINATING FACT: Fans sent 50,000 protest letters to Warner Bros. after Tim Burton announced the casting of Michael Keaton as Batman. 003 Han Solo APPEARANCES: Star Wars: A New Hope (1977), The Empire Strikes Back (1980), Return Of The Jedi (1983) CREATOR: George Lucas PERFORMER: Harrison Ford DEFINING MOMENT: Granted, Vader had the better wardrobe (black cape, motorcycle leathers), but Solo’s scruffy-looking smuggler still takes the gundark’s share of Star Wars cool. Shooting first (sorry George) and cracking wise, he’s every inch the space cowboy. The Quintessential Solo is heartfelt as well as cocksure, though, and never more so than in Ford’s famously ad-libbed response to Leia’s, “I love you,” in Episode V: “I know.” FASCINATING FACT: In Lucas’ early drafts of The Star Wars, Solo’s character was Ureallian: a noseless, green-skinned, slime-covered alien with large gills, who trapped Wookiees. Not quite so romantic now, is it? 002 James bond APPEARANCES: The James Bond series CREATOR: Ian Fleming PERFORMERS: Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, Daniel Craig DEFINING MOMENT: Probably varies by Bond — Moore unzipping Solitaire’s dress with a magnet would sum him up, for example, while Brosnan adjusting his tie after driving a tank through a wall nails him. But it was probably 007’s first film that laid out the marker for the next 50 years, when he shoots Professor Dent (“That’s a Smith & Wesson, and you’ve had your six”) with the insouciance of a man who’s just had a bid accepted on eBay. FASCINATING FACT: The Ian Fleming series of novels and shorts have been almost entirely mined for titles, but these remain available: Risico, The Hildebrand Rarity, The Property Of A Lady, and 007 In New York. They might remain unmined. 001 Indiana Jones APPEARANCES: All four Indiana Jones adventures (1981-2008) CREATORS: George Lucas, Lawrence Kasdan PERFORMER: Harrison Ford DEFINING MOMENT: The flicker of recognition that crosses Indy’s face when Belloq (Paul Freeman) suggests they are alike... Tied with the pained, “Do I really have to do this?” look he gives just before he shoots the Arab swordsman. FASCINATING FACT: It is common knowledge that Indiana Jones was originally called Indiana Smith, but changed to Jones at Spielberg’s behest. Yet the reason Spielberg wanted the seemingly negligible name change was to distance Raiders from Nevada Smith, a 1966 Steve McQueen Western. Movies Hattie Hook Boards Supernatural Thriller ‘Train’ From ‘The Conjuring’ Writers Published 3 weeks ago on November 6, 2025 By Meagan Navarro Hattie Hook in 'Of an Age' Hattie Hook ( Of An Age ) has boarded supernatural thriller Train , the directorial debut from Conjuring Universe scribes Chad and Carey Hayes , Deadline reports today. Hook joins previously announced cast member Frances O’Connor , who starred in The Conjuring 2 . Train follows “seventeen-year-old Katie Thompson, a troubled teen spiralling after the tragic death of her younger brother – a loss that has left her not only emotionally scarred but also cursed with a disturbing ability to glimpse the world beyond the living. Desperate to help her, Katie’s exhausted parents send her to a recovery centre, forcing her and her estranged mother, Tami, to board a long-distance train bound for Washington. “But as old tensions flare between them, Katie begins to experience terrifying visions and a ghostly presence warning of something sinister lurking aboard. What you need to know, whether you’re grieving or supporting a loved one. (Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) A cemetery in Huntsville. Brandon Palmer knows the holiday season has a double edge: It is happy and celebratory; a time when family and friends gather. But it can also be dark and painful for those experiencing grief and loss. Palmer is bereavement coordinator for Salt Lake City-based Intermountain Health. He and a small team of counselors provide grief support, counseling and education for people in Salt Lake and Utah counties. The Tribune asked Palmer how to best support people who are grieving during the holidays. Holly Mullen spoke with Palmer on behalf of The Salt Lake Tribune. Below is a Q&A that has been edited for length and clarity. Holly Mullen: Grief and loss are experiences no human can escape. What feelings can we expect upon the dying or death of a loved one, friend or even a beloved pet? Yes, grief is part of being human. None of us get through life untouched by it. People feel it in different ways, but sadness and yearning are almost always there. Anger, guilt, anxiety, and even relief can show up too, especially when someone has suffered for a long time. Many describe the early days of grief as surreal, like the world suddenly stopped making sense. And as time passes, the feelings don’t disappear, but they do shift. Love, gratitude and moments of peace and joy begin to weave themselves into the loss as well. Holly Mullen: There is science and data to support grief as a legitimate physical, mental and emotional condition, right? It’s not just in our head? Yes. Science now confirms what grieving people have always known, that loss affects the whole body. Neuroscientist Mary-Frances O’Connor, in her book “The Grieving Brain,” explains that grief activates the same parts of the brain that form our closest attachments. When someone dies, the brain struggles to update its internal “map,” which is why we sometimes reach for the phone to text them or expect to see them walk through the door. Her follow-up book, “The Grieving Body,” shows how grief shows up physically too: exhaustion, poor sleep, appetite changes, inflammation and a weakened immune system. Mentally, people often describe feeling foggy or forgetful. During grief, the body and brain try to find balance again after connection has been so disrupted. Holly Mullen: What is grief’s purpose? Grief is how we learn to live in a world that’s changed. It’s our mind and body’s way of recalibrating after a significant loss. Trauma and grief scholar George A. Bonanno says that sadness helps us slow down and reflect so we can absorb the reality of what’s happened. It gives us space to make sense of life without the person we love. At the same time, our sorrow shows in our faces, voices and gestures, signaling to others that we need care. In that way, grief can also help us receive empathy and connection from friends and family. Holly Mullen: Best way to approach someone who is grieving? There’s no perfect script for comforting someone who’s grieving. What feels comforting to one person can sting for another. But a few things are usually very unhelpful, especially phrases that start with “at least,” as in “at least they’re no longer suffering” or “at least you had time to say goodbye” can minimize their pain. A simple “I don’t know what to say, but I care about you” can mean more than anything rehearsed. Holly Mullen: If I am grieving this holiday season, what are the best things I can do for myself? Plan ahead. Think about which days or traditions might be hard and decide what you need, like quiet time, company or a mix of both. Honor the bond with your loved one. Light a candle, share memories, cook their favorite meal. Find small and simple ways to remember your loved one in ways that feel helpful for you. Make room for joy. Even if you don’t feel like it, find activities and people that help you feel moments of joy and meaning. Be gentle with yourself and lower expectations. Rest. Let people help. Honor old traditions and/or incorporate new ones as it feels helpful and comforting. Holly Mullen: When does grief go away? As renowned grief expert William Worden once noted, “ ‘When does grief go away?’ ” is a bit like asking “How high is up?’” Grief doesn’t ever really go away because love doesn’t ever go away. Holly Mullen: I’ve heard of something called “continuing bonds” in the grief process. Can you explain that? Continuing bonds are the ways we keep our loved ones close , even after they’re gone. Instead of “letting go,” we learn how to carry the relationship forward. Keeping certain items, maintaining familiar routines, or having quiet rituals, like talking to your loved one, visiting places that remind you of them, or simply thinking about them, are all natural ways people stay connected after a loss. Holly Mullen: Finally, Palmer offers a few good resources for people who are grieving or for their loved ones and friends . And Intermountain Health offers bereavement support, as well. He and a small team of counselors provide grief support, counseling and education for people in Salt Lake and Utah counties. Autumn is my favorite season, even though there are things I hate about it, like falling back from Daylight Saving Time. There is enough darkness in the world without giving it another hour. Still, fall in Arkansas means the oppressive heat of summer gives way to cooler weather, like taking the lid off a steaming pot. And I love pumpkins, hayrides, bonfires, soup, and hot chocolate. I like watching my daughter Stella play basketball. My yard stops needing to be mowed. I\'m wearing layers and snuggling in cozy covers. But most of all, I love the trees\' changing of the guard in all their colorful pageantry. The leaves across the river, like those that surround my house and form a canopy over my driveway, are at their peak. It is a riot of red, orange, yellow, and brown everywhere the light touches. I looked out the window and witnessed a flutter of them, as if this tree just released her bundle on cue. They floated to the ground like confetti, signaling the party is over. In a text conversation with an artist friend this morning, he said, "The leaves are changing, starting to die and fall to the ground. I used to worry about sweeping them up to clear the yard. Now I leave them to do their job and nurture the soil below. Why do we try and sweep away instead of letting it do its job and nurture our soul?" My instant answer to this question, which was probably rhetorical, was "pain." Like Pixar\'s Mr. Incredible, who saves the world every day and wishes it would just stay saved, I\'d like for my house to stay clean. I dislike the approach of darkness at 5:30 p.m. I wish the laundry could stay done. And I would like to think I have reached my quota for pain and loss. But this is not how the world works. And I feel guilty even typing that because there are people I know--as well as people all over the world--who suffer to far greater degrees than I can even fathom. What can be done about it? Eastern traditions tell us there\'s really no such thing as pain; we create it by how we respond to circumstances. The ideal seems to be detachment, an open-handed approach that doesn\'t hold onto anything or anyone too tightly. Stoics like Marcus Aurelius agree and take it a step further to teach the concept of amor fati--the choice to love your fate. Embrace whatever comes without labeling it good or bad, pain or non-pain. The point is to discipline your mind and pay attention to what fate can reveal that makes you stronger. I think there are echoes of this in Christianity. Verses that instruct us to "rejoice always," and "count it all joy" come to mind. Lately, I have taken comfort in an unusual place: neuroscience. It can be helpful to understand that grieving, our response to pain, originates in the evolution of our brains. There is a purpose for it rooted in our need for safety and survival. So even though sometimes it feels like grief will kill us, nature actually intends the opposite. As humans formed deep social bonds in order to thrive as a species, grief became a necessity. Because ultimately the internal system of grief motivates us to seek those bonds again, even after the pain of losing them, by taking us through a cycle much like the falling leaves. When grief happens, it is an all-body event. It affects our limbic system, suppresses immunity, dumps cortisol in waves. Our bodies react like this to force us to withdraw and rest. It is all temporary, or should be in healthy people, to help us survive and recover. We must allow our system to reset. This is when we let the leaves be, and allow them to do their quiet work. When we lose a connection important to our survival, grief pushes us to update our internal model of the world. We have to rewire expectations, habits, and identity structures. Our brains have a biological drive toward psychological coherence, so when we experience loss we try to make sense out of it and integrate that experience into our internal model. This meaning-making stage is messy, and not particularly linear. But it is an actual biological phenomenon, not entirely a spiritual one, not entirely our choice, either, since it is in our DNA. The social function of grief is that after we are re-integrated at least to a point, we tend to signal a need for social support. This brings us full circle to create new bonds and continue surviving individually and as a species. Mary-Frances O\'Connor describes a lot of this in her book "The Grieving Brain." When our brains evolved thousands of years ago, the world was haunted by food scarcity and predators, and being separated from others was dangerous. Separation instantly sounded alarms via our limbic systems so we would find them again and be safe. Even though we can survive more easily now--working from home and ordering take-out--we are still hardwired to nurture relationships, and when we experience an important loss, our paleo brain signals alarm. It is the tough price we pay for human attachment. When spring comes with new life and light, we tend to decide it\'s all worth it. Even if the next fall is just around the corner. Neuroscience tells us that so is the next spring. The important thing for survival is to keep going. Gwen Ford Faulkenberry is an author, teacher, and award-winning columnist from Ozark. In the era of Game of Thrones and now Britannia , you can see why somebody fancied having a go at the swords-sandals-and-sorcery of the Trojan War. The question is, how? A dash of instant lustre has been added in the shape of screenwriter David Farr, who also wrote the much-admired adaptation of The Night Manager . However, early enthusiasm is liable to fade in the face of the beige-ish characterisations and mundane dialogue with which Farr has littered his stage, while a largely unknown cast lacking big personalities who might dominate the screen doesn’t help much. Having characters in robes and carrying swords amid gods, goddesses and mythic scenery, yet talking like normal folks waiting for a bus or down the supermarket, leaves the action feeling starved of dramatic wattage. There is, at least, David Threlfall bringing a modicum of gravitas to the role of Troy’s King Priam, while his wife Hecuba is sympathetically played by Mrs Selfridge, Frances O’Connor (pictured right with Threlfall) . This opening episode kicked off with Hecuba undergoing a gruesome childbirth involving a red-hot knife and buckets of blood (did nobody think to call the midwife?), so it was a miracle the child survived. The omens were not good, however – when young Cassandra caught a glimpse of her new baby brother, she instantly had a vision of a fiery apocalypse and suffered a screaming fit. Though we don’t know it at first, the baby boy grows up to be Paris (Louis Hunter), whom we next encounter as a kind of classical cowboy, rounding up cattle on horseback amid rugged and mountainous landscapes ( Troy was shot near Cape Town). Pursuing a missing calf through a wood, he happens upon Hermes and a trio of goddesses. Zeus, the big enchilada of Olympus and grumpily played by Hakeem Kae-Kazim (pictured below) , had decided that Paris must choose which of the goddesses is the loveliest (he had to pick up a flaming apple from a fire to give to the winner, and miraculously did so without feeling any pain). Frankly they looked more like C-list celebrities trying to gate-crash an Oscar night party than goddesses, but he chose Aphrodite, because she promised to give him the world’s most beautiful woman in return. You can see the way this is going, even if Farr has played a tiny bit fast and loose with the accepted mythology. Paris is the royal son who (in this version) was stolen away by wolves as a baby, but now returns to take up his birthright. His dad packs him off in the royal yacht to ink a mutually-beneficial pact with Sparta’s King Menelaus (Jonas Armstrong), but Paris, an untutored youth who hasn’t a clue about politics, diplomacy and so forth, becomes fixated on Menelaus’s wife, Helen (remember that name). Playing Helen is a big ask for any actress, she being the world’s most beauteous woman who will in due course launch 1,000 ships etc, and Bella Dayne does it here… kind of okay, I guess. A glimpse of her with what appears to be her private lesbian harem gets Paris’s sap rising, and before you know it she has lured him out to her leafy private boudoir in the palace grounds. Paris must return to Troy, though Helen is feeling too tired to see him off. But what do you think might be inside the huge trunk that is sent down to his ship? Answers please in a mystical vision of fire, sword, passion and computer-generated navies. Austenâ\x80\x99s settingsâ\x80\x94grand ballrooms, lively Regency towns, and vast country estatesâ\x80\x94were inspired by many real places she visited in her lifetime, and numerous locations across England have served as backdrops in the movie and TV versions of Austenâ\x80\x99s works. What you need to know, whether you’re grieving or supporting a loved one. (Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) A cemetery in Huntsville. Brandon Palmer knows the holiday season has a double edge: It is happy and celebratory; a time when family and friends gather. But it can also be dark and painful for those experiencing grief and loss. Palmer is bereavement coordinator for Salt Lake City-based Intermountain Health. He and a small team of counselors provide grief support, counseling and education for people in Salt Lake and Utah counties. The Tribune asked Palmer how to best support people who are grieving during the holidays. Holly Mullen spoke with Palmer on behalf of The Salt Lake Tribune. Below is a Q&A that has been edited for length and clarity. Holly Mullen: Grief and loss are experiences no human can escape. What feelings can we expect upon the dying or death of a loved one, friend or even a beloved pet? Yes, grief is part of being human. None of us get through life untouched by it. People feel it in different ways, but sadness and yearning are almost always there. Anger, guilt, anxiety, and even relief can show up too, especially when someone has suffered for a long time. Many describe the early days of grief as surreal, like the world suddenly stopped making sense. And as time passes, the feelings don’t disappear, but they do shift. Love, gratitude and moments of peace and joy begin to weave themselves into the loss as well. Holly Mullen: There is science and data to support grief as a legitimate physical, mental and emotional condition, right? It’s not just in our head? Yes. Science now confirms what grieving people have always known, that loss affects the whole body. Neuroscientist Mary-Frances O’Connor, in her book “The Grieving Brain,” explains that grief activates the same parts of the brain that form our closest attachments. When someone dies, the brain struggles to update its internal “map,” which is why we sometimes reach for the phone to text them or expect to see them walk through the door. Her follow-up book, “The Grieving Body,” shows how grief shows up physically too: exhaustion, poor sleep, appetite changes, inflammation and a weakened immune system. Mentally, people often describe feeling foggy or forgetful. During grief, the body and brain try to find balance again after connection has been so disrupted. Holly Mullen: What is grief’s purpose? Grief is how we learn to live in a world that’s changed. It’s our mind and body’s way of recalibrating after a significant loss. Trauma and grief scholar George A. Bonanno says that sadness helps us slow down and reflect so we can absorb the reality of what’s happened. It gives us space to make sense of life without the person we love. At the same time, our sorrow shows in our faces, voices and gestures, signaling to others that we need care. In that way, grief can also help us receive empathy and connection from friends and family. Holly Mullen: Best way to approach someone who is grieving? There’s no perfect script for comforting someone who’s grieving. What feels comforting to one person can sting for another. But a few things are usually very unhelpful, especially phrases that start with “at least,” as in “at least they’re no longer suffering” or “at least you had time to say goodbye” can minimize their pain. A simple “I don’t know what to say, but I care about you” can mean more than anything rehearsed. Holly Mullen: If I am grieving this holiday season, what are the best things I can do for myself? Plan ahead. Think about which days or traditions might be hard and decide what you need, like quiet time, company or a mix of both. Honor the bond with your loved one. Light a candle, share memories, cook their favorite meal. Find small and simple ways to remember your loved one in ways that feel helpful for you. Make room for joy. Even if you don’t feel like it, find activities and people that help you feel moments of joy and meaning. Be gentle with yourself and lower expectations. Rest. Let people help. Honor old traditions and/or incorporate new ones as it feels helpful and comforting. Holly Mullen: When does grief go away? As renowned grief expert William Worden once noted, “ ‘When does grief go away?’ ” is a bit like asking “How high is up?’” Grief doesn’t ever really go away because love doesn’t ever go away. Holly Mullen: I’ve heard of something called “continuing bonds” in the grief process. Can you explain that? Continuing bonds are the ways we keep our loved ones close , even after they’re gone. Instead of “letting go,” we learn how to carry the relationship forward. Keeping certain items, maintaining familiar routines, or having quiet rituals, like talking to your loved one, visiting places that remind you of them, or simply thinking about them, are all natural ways people stay connected after a loss. Holly Mullen: Finally, Palmer offers a few good resources for people who are grieving or for their loved ones and friends . And Intermountain Health offers bereavement support, as well. Autumn is my favorite season, even though there are things I hate about it, like falling back from Daylight Saving Time. There is enough darkness in the world without giving it another hour. Still, fall in Arkansas means the oppressive heat of summer gives way to cooler weather, like taking the lid off a steaming pot. And I love pumpkins, hayrides, bonfires, soup, and hot chocolate. I like watching my daughter Stella play basketball. My yard stops needing to be mowed. I\'m wearing layers and snuggling in cozy covers. But most of all, I love the trees\' changing of the guard in all their colorful pageantry. The leaves across the river, like those that surround my house and form a canopy over my driveway, are at their peak. It is a riot of red, orange, yellow, and brown everywhere the light touches. I looked out the window and witnessed a flutter of them, as if this tree just released her bundle on cue. They floated to the ground like confetti, signaling the party is over. In a text conversation with an artist friend this morning, he said, "The leaves are changing, starting to die and fall to the ground. I used to worry about sweeping them up to clear the yard. Now I leave them to do their job and nurture the soil below. Why do we try and sweep away instead of letting it do its job and nurture our soul?" My instant answer to this question, which was probably rhetorical, was "pain." Like Pixar\'s Mr. Incredible, who saves the world every day and wishes it would just stay saved, I\'d like for my house to stay clean. I dislike the approach of darkness at 5:30 p.m. I wish the laundry could stay done. And I would like to think I have reached my quota for pain and loss. But this is not how the world works. And I feel guilty even typing that because there are people I know--as well as people all over the world--who suffer to far greater degrees than I can even fathom. What can be done about it? Eastern traditions tell us there\'s really no such thing as pain; we create it by how we respond to circumstances. The ideal seems to be detachment, an open-handed approach that doesn\'t hold onto anything or anyone too tightly. Stoics like Marcus Aurelius agree and take it a step further to teach the concept of amor fati--the choice to love your fate. Embrace whatever comes without labeling it good or bad, pain or non-pain. The point is to discipline your mind and pay attention to what fate can reveal that makes you stronger. I think there are echoes of this in Christianity. Verses that instruct us to "rejoice always," and "count it all joy" come to mind. Lately, I have taken comfort in an unusual place: neuroscience. It can be helpful to understand that grieving, our response to pain, originates in the evolution of our brains. There is a purpose for it rooted in our need for safety and survival. So even though sometimes it feels like grief will kill us, nature actually intends the opposite. As humans formed deep social bonds in order to thrive as a species, grief became a necessity. Because ultimately the internal system of grief motivates us to seek those bonds again, even after the pain of losing them, by taking us through a cycle much like the falling leaves. When grief happens, it is an all-body event. It affects our limbic system, suppresses immunity, dumps cortisol in waves. Our bodies react like this to force us to withdraw and rest. It is all temporary, or should be in healthy people, to help us survive and recover. We must allow our system to reset. This is when we let the leaves be, and allow them to do their quiet work. When we lose a connection important to our survival, grief pushes us to update our internal model of the world. We have to rewire expectations, habits, and identity structures. Our brains have a biological drive toward psychological coherence, so when we experience loss we try to make sense out of it and integrate that experience into our internal model. This meaning-making stage is messy, and not particularly linear. But it is an actual biological phenomenon, not entirely a spiritual one, not entirely our choice, either, since it is in our DNA. The social function of grief is that after we are re-integrated at least to a point, we tend to signal a need for social support. This brings us full circle to create new bonds and continue surviving individually and as a species. Mary-Frances O\'Connor describes a lot of this in her book "The Grieving Brain." When our brains evolved thousands of years ago, the world was haunted by food scarcity and predators, and being separated from others was dangerous. Separation instantly sounded alarms via our limbic systems so we would find them again and be safe. Even though we can survive more easily now--working from home and ordering take-out--we are still hardwired to nurture relationships, and when we experience an important loss, our paleo brain signals alarm. It is the tough price we pay for human attachment. When spring comes with new life and light, we tend to decide it\'s all worth it. Even if the next fall is just around the corner. Neuroscience tells us that so is the next spring. The important thing for survival is to keep going. Gwen Ford Faulkenberry is an author, teacher, and award-winning columnist from Ozark. Soapification of The Trojan War reviews, news & interviews Troy: Fall of a City, BBC One review - soapification of the Trojan War Classical myth reborn as low-voltage melodrama by Adam Sweeting Sunday, February 18, 2018 share this article Share The plan to bring drama back to Saturday nights on BBC One enjoyed mixed success with Hard Sun , but now threatens to slide over a cliff with this trip back to the Homeric era. In the era of Game of Thrones and now Britannia , you can see why somebody fancied having a go at the swords-sandals-and-sorcery of the Trojan War. The question is, how? A dash of instant lustre has been added in the shape of screenwriter David Farr, who also wrote the much-admired adaptation of The Night Manager . However, early enthusiasm is liable to fade in the face of the beige-ish characterisations and mundane dialogue with which Farr has littered his stage, while a largely unknown cast lacking big personalities who might dominate the screen doesn’t help much. Having characters in robes and carrying swords amid gods, goddesses and mythic scenery, yet talking like normal folks waiting for a bus or down the supermarket, leaves the action feeling starved of dramatic wattage. There is, at least, David Threlfall bringing a modicum of gravitas to the role of Troy’s King Priam, while his wife Hecuba is sympathetically played by Mrs Selfridge, Frances O’Connor (pictured right with Threlfall) . This opening episode kicked off with Hecuba undergoing a gruesome childbirth involving a red-hot knife and buckets of blood (did nobody think to call the midwife?), so it was a miracle the child survived. The omens were not good, however – when young Cassandra caught a glimpse of her new baby brother, she instantly had a vision of a fiery apocalypse and suffered a screaming fit. Though we don’t know it at first, the baby boy grows up to be Paris (Louis Hunter), whom we next encounter as a kind of classical cowboy, rounding up cattle on horseback amid rugged and mountainous landscapes ( Troy was shot near Cape Town). Pursuing a missing calf through a wood, he happens upon Hermes and a trio of goddesses. Zeus, the big enchilada of Olympus and grumpily played by Hakeem Kae-Kazim (pictured below) , had decided that Paris must choose which of the goddesses is the loveliest (he had to pick up a flaming apple from a fire to give to the winner, and miraculously did so without feeling any pain). Frankly they looked more like C-list celebrities trying to gate-crash an Oscar night party than goddesses, but he chose Aphrodite, because she promised to give him the world’s most beautiful woman in return. You can see the way this is going, even if Farr has played a tiny bit fast and loose with the accepted mythology. Paris is the royal son who (in this version) was stolen away by wolves as a baby, but now returns to take up his birthright. His dad packs him off in the royal yacht to ink a mutually-beneficial pact with Sparta’s King Menelaus (Jonas Armstrong), but Paris, an untutored youth who hasn’t a clue about politics, diplomacy and so forth, becomes fixated on Menelaus’s wife, Helen (remember that name). Playing Helen is a big ask for any actress, she being the world’s most beauteous woman who will in due course launch 1,000 ships etc, and Bella Dayne does it here… kind of okay, I guess. A glimpse of her with what appears to be her private lesbian harem gets Paris’s sap rising, and before you know it she has lured him out to her leafy private boudoir in the palace grounds. Paris must return to Troy, though Helen is feeling too tired to see him off. But what do you think might be inside the huge trunk that is sent down to his ship? Answers please in a mystical vision of fire, sword, passion and computer-generated navies. By Claire Cock-Starkey | Share on Facebook Share on X Copy Article A view of Chatsworth House, known to Jane Austen fans as Mr. Darcyâ\x80\x99s Pemberley. | Christopher Furlong/Getty Images Share on Facebook Share on X Share on Reddit Copy Article December 2025 marks the 250th anniversary of the birth of Jane Austen. Her six completed novels have become canon, inspiring numerous adaptations into TV series and films. Austenâ\x80\x99s settingsâ\x80\x94grand ballrooms, lively Regency towns, and vast country estatesâ\x80\x94were inspired by many real places she visited in her lifetime, and numerous locations across England have served as backdrops in the movie and TV versions of Austenâ\x80\x99s works. Today, itâ\x80\x99s possible to visit and imagine yourself an Austen hero (or villain!).Â Below are eight Jane Austen movie locationsâ\x80\x94and two bonus locations associated with Austenâ\x80\x99s lifeâ\x80\x94that you can visit in person. Box Hill, Surrey // Emma Lyme Regis, Dorset // Persuasion Montacute House, Somerset // Sense and Sensibility Claydon House, Buckinghamshire // Emma Lyme Park, Cheshire // Pride and Prejudice Chatsworth House, Derbyshire // Pride and Prejudice Kirby Hall, Northamptonshire // Mansfield Park The City of Bath // Northanger Abbey and Persuasion Bonus: Jane Austenâ\x80\x99s Home and Her Burial PlaceÂ Box Hill, Surrey // Emma Picnickers enjoy Box Hill in Surrey. | Alex Burstow/GettyImages In Emma , a famous picnic scene at Box Hill in Surrey takes place in which the title character behaves rudely and is taken to task for her aloofness. The real Box Hill is in an area of Outstanding Natural Beauty in the Surrey Hills. Visitors can climb the hill, explore the ancient woodland, and enjoy the panoramic views. However, those wishing to recreate the picnic as depicted in both the 2009 mini-series of Emma (featuring Romola Garai) or the 2020 movie adaptation (featuring Anya Taylor-Joy) would need to visit Leith Hill , just 10 miles away from Box Hill. Leith Hill enjoys the same rolling hills and expansive views but has the added cachÃ© of a link to Charles Darwin. Darwin frequently enjoyed walks on Leith Hill with his sister, and a stone in the grounds (today known as the â\x80\x9c worm stone â\x80\x9d) inspired his theory that ancient stones sank into the earth thanks to the action of earthworms. Lyme Regis, Dorset // Persuasion Lyme Regis in Dorset. | Gavin Hellier/robertharding/Collection Mix: Subjects/Getty Images Jane Austen visited Lyme Regis in Dorset on at least two occasions in 1803 and 1804, and the seaside town clearly caught her imagination because she featured it in her final novel, Persuasion . The town has a number of spots associated with Austen that you can explore, including a human-made stone addition to the harbor wall known as the Cobb . It is here that Louisa Musgrove falls and is helped by the dashing Captain Wentworth in the novel, and the scene was filmed at the location for the 2022 Netflix version of Persuasion starring Dakota Johnson. Lyme Regis Museum also has a number of Austen items in its collection, and thereâ\x80\x99s a lovely Jane Austen Garden, built as a memorial, that offers wonderful views of the bay. Austen fans will also be delighted to see the blue plaque above the door of Pyne House on Broad Street , which reads, â\x80\x9cThis is the most likely lodging of Jane Austen, whose visits to Lyme in 1803 and 1804Â gave birth to her novel Persuasion .â\x80\x9d You May Also Like ... 5 of the Best Jane Austen Adaptations See What Pride and Prejudice's Mr. Darcy Really Looks Like Jane Austen, Home Brewer Add Mental Floss as a Â preferred news source ! Montacute House, Somerset // Sense and Sensibility Montacute House in Somerset. | Mike Searle / Montacute House East Front, Wikimedia Commons // CC BY-SA 2.0 This handsome house in Somerset was built in 1598 and is one of the few grand houses in England that has remained relatively unchanged since Elizabethan times. As a result, itâ\x80\x99s been a popular filming location , seen in Johnny Deppâ\x80\x99s The Libertine (2004), the recent BBC adaptation of Hilary Mantelâ\x80\x99s Wolf Hall , and the 1995 adaptation of Austenâ\x80\x99s Sense and Sensibility starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet. The impressive house stood in as the home of the Palmers; its extensive gardens appeared in a scene in which heartbroken Marianne falls ill after walking through the rain. Claydon House, Buckinghamshire // Emma Claydon House in Buckinghamshire. | Nigel Cox / Claydon House, Wikimedia Commons // CC BY-SA 2.0 Austenâ\x80\x99s novels are well known for their depiction of glorious galas, and in Emma , a key scene takes place on the dancefloor at the fictional Donwell Abbey in which Harriet is cruelly snubbed by Mr. Elton. The 1996 film starring Gwyneth Paltrow as the titular character filmed the scene in the beautiful yellow and white rococo North Hall of Claydon House . In what could be a plot from an Austen novel itself, the extraordinary lavish interior of the house was commissioned by wealthy nobleman Ralph Verney in the 1750s in an effort to demonstrate his status and eclipse the homes of his equally wealthy neighbors. His expensive taste and ambitious plans led to his eventual financial ruin, but the gorgeous and over-the-top interiors remain. Lyme Park, Cheshire // Pride and Prejudice Lyme Park in Cheshire. | Heritage Images/GettyImages The most iconic home in all of Austenâ\x80\x99s novels is Mr. Darcyâ\x80\x99s Pemberley. Austen describes it in loving detail and itâ\x80\x99s easy to see why the grand estate beguiles Lizzie. Itâ\x80\x99s where she encounters the dashing Mr. Darcy, though the scene in which the character, played by Colin Firth, emerges soaking wet after a swim in the lake was invented for the 1995 BBC adaptation of Pride and Prejudice . That memorable exchange was filmed at Lyme Park , Cheshire, where the stunning house is set in acres of serene parkland, but it turns out Firth never did dive into the lake . Producers were too worried he might catch something from the water, so a stuntman took his place, and Firthâ\x80\x99s wet-look shirt and tousled hair were achieved with the help of a generous spritz of water. Chatsworth House, Derbyshire // Pride and Prejudice The South Front of Chatsworth in Derbyshire. | Rprof, Wikimedia Commons // CC BY-SA 3.0 In the other major Pride and Prejudice production, the 2005 movie starring Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen, Chatsworth in Derbyshire stood in for Pemberley. Chatsworth may have inspired Austenâ\x80\x99s vision of the â\x80\x9chandsomeâ\x80\x9d stone house, and itâ\x80\x99s mentioned as a location that Lizzie visits while in Derbyshire. The bust of Matthew Macfadyen that was created for the scene in which Mr. Darcyâ\x80\x99s housekeeper tells Lizzie of his many good qualities is on display at Chatsworth, reminding visitors of its key role in the movie. Chatsworth is now a major visitor attraction thanks to its renovations by the Duchess of Devonshire , Deborah Mitford, the youngest of the famous Mitford sisters .Â Â Kirby Hall, Northamptonshire // Mansfield Park Kirby Hall in Northamptonshire. | Angelo Hornak/GettyImages Kirby Hall in Northamptonshire was used as the titular location in the 1999 movie adaptation starring Frances Oâ\x80\x99Connor and Jonny Lee Miller. A medieval house had stood for many years on the site, but it wasnâ\x80\x99t until 1570 that Sir Humphrey Stafford ordered a new grand house to be built, his reason being that Queen Elizabeth I visited the area and had to stay with one of his neighbors because Stafford did not have the room to accommodate her. The house was remodeled in the 17th century, creating a beautifully symmetrical Jacobean frontage and the perfect stand-in for Austenâ\x80\x99s Mansfield Park. The City of Bath // Northanger Abbey and Persuasion A view of Bath. | joe daniel price/Moment/Getty Images Jane Austen lived in Bath from 1801 to 1806, and its sweeping crescents and honey-colored Georgian houses inspired Austen to set both Persuasion and Northanger Abbey in the city. Bath made multiple appearances in the 1995 BBC production and the 2022 Netflix version of Persuasion . The famous Royal Crescent , Bath Street, Brock Street, and Gravel Walk all provided sumptuous backdrops for the recent Netflix adaptation. Bath has become strongly associated with Austen because she mentions the city in all six of her novels. Visitors to Bath can see filming locations as well as explore the Jane Austen Centre , a charming Georgian house where visitors can experience what life was like in Regency Bath. Bonus: Jane Austenâ\x80\x99s Home and Her Burial PlaceÂ Chawton, Hampshire // Jane Austenâ\x80\x99s House Jane Austen's House in Chawton, Hampshire. | Heritage Images/GettyImages Jane Austen lived in a cottage in Chawton, Hampshire, from 1809 until her death in 1817. It was in this house that Austen wrote all six of her world-famous novels, and it has been transformed into a museum dedicated to her life and works. Visitors can see her writing table, first editions of her books, and personal items such as jewelry, dresses, and letters to her beloved sister, Cassandra. Winchester Cathedral, Hampshire // Austenâ\x80\x99s Burial Place Austenâ\x80\x99s memorial stone in Winchester Cathedral. | Patrick Denker , Flickr // CC BY 2.0 Austen became ill about a year before she died at the age of 41, and in the last months of her life she traveled to Winchester for treatment. Medical historians have long debated the cause of Austenâ\x80\x99s death . Some posthumous diagnoses include from Addisonâ\x80\x99s disease, Hodgkinâ\x80\x99s disease, or lupus. Whatever the cause, her final months were grim , and when her sister asked if she needed anything she resorted to a quote from The Pilgrimâ\x80\x99s Progress : â\x80\x9cnothing but death.â\x80\x9dÂ She passed away on July 18, 1817, and was buried in Winchester Cathedral on July 24. Her burial stone can be seen in the floor of the north nave of the cathedral, but it makes no mention of her writing, so a brass plaque was added in 1872 that details her significance as a writer. Hundreds of visitors a year come to pay respects at her grave and leave small offerings such as letters or flowersâ\x80\x94a testament to the many lives her work has touched. Whether it was a dark connection between a psychiatrist and a serial killer in Hannibal or between a woman and her former kidnapper in Found , some of the most fascinating relationships are often the most complex ones. It might be difficult to always understand the dynamics in a toxic game of cat-and-mouse , but the pull towards someone or something that might be bad for you is actually pretty relatable. One of the most intriguing and tangled partnerships from the last 10 years also happens to be from one of the best spy thrillers that should be added to your must-watch list right away. Luckily, it is free to stream on Tubi . What Is \'Killing Eve\' About? Jodie Comer as Villanelle holds a knife to Sandra Oh as Eve in the kitchen in Killing Eve. Image via BBC America Killing Eve , which aired on BBC America for four seasons from 2018 to 2022, is a fantastic blend of spy drama and dark comedy. Based on the Villanelle novellas by Luke Jennings , each of the four seasons was led by a different female head writer. With brilliant writers such as Phoebe Waller-Bridge and Emerald Fennell , the series was always going to be both electric and smart. In the first season , we meet Eve Polastri ( Sandra Oh ), an American spy living in the U.K., who gets fired from her MI5 role after going rogue. She ends up being drafted to join a secret division within MI6, and is tasked with locating one of the most dangerous international assassins out there. Most assassins in spy thrillers fall into the same male stereotype, but Killing Eve\' s ruthless killer is anything but typical. Villanelle ( Jodie Comer ) is a young, pretty woman who works for a secret organization called The Twelve. She manages to fly under the radar ( and successfully take out her targets ) precisely because she doesn\'t fit the mold and catches most of her victims completely unaware. When Eve finally locates Villanelle, and the two cross paths, what unfolds is a continuous cycle of danger as both women become increasingly obsessed with each other. Related Sandra Oh & Jodie Comer’s Acclaimed Spy Thriller ‘Killing Eve’ Is Streaming for Free for the First Time "Sorry baby." Posts 2 By Lade Omotade Jan 21, 2025 As each season unfolds, we learn more about both of these main characters. Eve feels suffocated in her marriage to the kind-hearted Niko ( Owen McDonnell ), who doesn\'t really seem to be able to give Eve the excitement she\'s craving. And then there\'s Villanelle, who is one of the most unique anti-heroes ever written. She takes immense pleasure in her kills , and doesn\'t seem to have an empathetic bone in her body. It\'s difficult for her to relate to people in a normal way, but somehow she can connect to Eve. Villanelle is also pretty funny, and offers Killing Eve much of its comedic relief. She has a fascinating relationship with her handler , a Russian man named Konstantin Vasiliev ( Kim Bodnia ), who is perpetually frustrated by his inability to rein Villanelle in. Each character weaves together a narrative to create a dangerous and intriguing world for the series to play around in. \'Killing Eve\' Depicts One of the Wildest Cat-and-Mouse Games Ever In all 32 episodes, Eve and Villanelle find themselves getting drawn back to each other , which develops a seductive vibe that the series thrives on. Every interaction they have sparks with electricity, and it\'s clear from the start that Oh and Comer have incredibly impressive chemistry . They\'re also able to depict a suspenseful, intricate tone that dances between impressive fight sequences and quiet moments of intimacy between characters . The series sets a fast-paced tone that still somehow allows the viewer to feel a connection to the characters (in between chases and murders, of course). In this cat-and-mouse game between Eve and Villanelle, it can be difficult to discern who\'s the hero sometimes. It often feels difficult to root for a terrifying killer , but Villanelle somehow still manages to steal hearts. Both women display questionable choices on their journeys, but this only serves to make the series become one of the sexiest, most unpredictable shows around. Sandra Oh and Jodie Comer Make \'Killing Eve\' an Electrifying Ride From Start to Finish Eve (Sandra Oh) and Villanelle (Jodie Comer) standing, with an aquarium between them in \'Killing Eve\' Image via BBC America Killing Eve is worthy of a bing because of the incredible writing (especially in the first two seasons). But the show would not have been as successful as it was without the truly remarkable performances from Oh and Comer. Oh had already been an established actor (from her time over on Grey\'s Anatomy ), but Comer wasn\'t well-known before Killing Eve . Her portrayal of Villanelle is one-of-a-kind, twisted, masterpiece. Future seasons explore more of Villanelle\'s past, which allows us to better understand how she ends up where she is, and Comer illustrates every stage of Villanelle\'s life with the same combination of playfulness and grit. The two actors\' chemistry together makes Killing Eve a series that depicts the ultimate toxic partnership , but one that is hard to turn away from. The leads in Killing Eve are incredible, but the supporting cast is nothing to sneeze at either. Fiona Shaw is the stoic and hard-nosed head of MI6 named Carolyn Martens. Her brisk iciness (and eventual thawing) brings another level of intrigue to the series. Bodnia becomes a throughline of humor as Villanelle\'s handler, and despite his position as someone who is basically facilitating murders, somehow becomes sort of lovable. Harriet Walter is also a stand-out in Season 3 , as Dasha Duzran, Villanelle\'s former mentor. Her plotline is a memorable one, and only elevates the series\' always-entertaining storytelling style. Each minor character helps to support the leads so that the web of mystery and suspense becomes even more captivating. Killing Eve wrapped up Eve and Villanelle\'s stories with a fourth and final season. While some fans weren\'t necessarily happy with where Killing Eve \'s characters ended up (no spoilers here), the entire show is worthy of a watch for its action-packed storylines and edgy performances. Killing Eve had a far-reaching influence, especially Villanelle\'s glamorous clothes, which inspired several real-life fashion trends . The series also managed to snag 21 Emmy nominations during its run, with Comer deservedly picking up a statue in 2019. Killing Eve is definitely not your average romance or a spy thriller like the ones you\'ve seen before. Rather, this twisted tale with morally ambiguous characters is a show that you\'ll soon find yourself obsessed with . It\'s also free to watch right now on Tubi, so you have no excuse not to dive in. Bugonia and Good Fortune close their theatrical run with strong reviews but weak earnings—here’s how much Bugonia must make in North America to beat Keanu Reeves’ comedy flop. By Arunava Chakrabarty - November 22, 2025 | 3:06 PM IST Follow Us Join Us Bugonia North America Box Office(Photo Credit –Facebook) Bugonia and Good Fortune have been drifting through their final days on the big screen with a strange sense of shared fate, almost like two films walking side by side, even though they were never meant to. Both arrived with critic support, strong ratings, and had big names leading the charge. Keanu Reeves powered one, Emma Stone carried the other, and everything looked lined up for a smooth theatrical journey. What followed instead turned out to be something far less flattering for the box office charts. Bugonia Slips Despite Strong Reviews Bugonia opened on October 24 with the confidence of a $55 million production behind it. The numbers looked promising for a moment, then slowly settled into a pattern that became hard to ignore. The worldwide gross has only crawled a little above $32.2 million. The domestic side sits at $16.3 million, while the international total lingers at $15.8 million, forming a picture that no studio dreams of, as per Box Office Mojo . For Yorgos Lanthimos, it still became the third-highest-grossing title in his career, yet the overall performance has fallen far below expectations. With its theater count now reduced to around 1,250 screens across the US, daily earnings are roughly $100K. By Thursday, the per-screen average slipped to $85, the lowest since release, showing that the downward curve has settled firmly in place. With a leaner $30 million production budget, one could have hoped for a safer margin, but the worldwide total has stalled at $25 million. The cast included Keanu Reeves, Aziz Ansari, Seth Rogen, and Sandra Oh, yet the enthusiasm from audiences never translated into tickets. The film’s domestic tally stands near $16.5 million, while overseas numbers stretch to a faint $8.8 million. Its presence in US theaters has shrunk to around 200 screens, where it brings in a few thousand dollars daily. By Thursday, its per-theater average sat at $31. Good Fortune Box Office Summary North America – $16.5 million International – $8.8 million Worldwide- $25.4 million A Tiny Gap Separates Their Domestic Totals When the two films are placed side by side, Good Fortune edges ahead of Bugonia in domestic performance by a slight margin of around $22K, which translates to a lead of only 1.3%. With its wider theatrical presence, Bugonia may bridge this gap within a day or two, but that shift will barely impact the larger outcome. Both titles have settled into the same corner, two films that arrived with promise and attention, yet faded into the list of this year’s most noticeable underperformers.
